content: A first professional degree is an academic qualification specifically designed to prepare individuals for a particular profession. These degrees focus on practical skills rather than theoretical or analytical knowledge. Professions that typically require such degrees are often regulated or licensed by governmental or government-approved bodies. Examples of these professions include medicine, law, architecture, engineering, dentistry, pharmacy, optometry, social work, religious ministry, and education, among others. First professional degrees can be awarded at either the undergraduate or graduate level, depending on the field and country. In the United States, the naming of certain professional degrees as doctorates originated as a way to reflect the advanced nature of the training. For instance, U.S. law schools transitioned from awarding the Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) to the Juris Doctor (J.D.), and medical schools shifted from the Bachelor of Medicine (M.B.) to the Doctor of Medicine (M.D.). This trend has also influenced other fields, such as physical therapy, where programs in the U.S. are moving from bachelor's or master's degrees to the Doctor of Physical Therapy (D.P.T.). Globally, many countries still reserve the title of doctorate for advanced academic research degrees, such as the Ph.D. However, in the U.S., some professional degrees, like the M.D., J.D., and Doctor of Dental Surgery (D.D.S.), are considered first professional degrees and are distinct from research doctorates. For example, a British medical degree (MBBS) is considered equivalent to the U.S. M.D., and individuals with an MBBS practicing in the U.S. are allowed to use the title M.D. In medicine, the first professional degree varies by country. It may be a Bachelor of Medicine and Surgery (MBBS, MBChB), a Doctor of Medicine (M.D. in the U.S. or MDCM in Canada), or a Dr. med. in Germany. Advanced professional degrees in medicine include the Master of Science (e.g., in Surgery) or research doctorates like the Ph.D. in medical sciences. Similarly, in law, the first professional degree may be a Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.), Bachelor of Civil Law (B.C.L.), or Juris Doctor (J.D.), while the terminal academic research degree could be a Doctor of Juridical Science (J.S.D.) or a Ph.D. in law. In engineering, the first professional degree is often a Bachelor of Engineering (B.E.), Bachelor of Applied Science (B.A.Sc.), or Bachelor of Science in Engineering (B.S.E.), depending on the country. Advanced professional degrees include the Master of Engineering (M.Eng.), while terminal research degrees include the Ph.D., Doctor of Science (Sc.D.), or Doctor of Engineering (D.Eng.). In the Netherlands, students can pursue a Professional Doctorate in Engineering (PDEng) as an alternative to a Ph.D. Some professional fields, such as architecture and fine arts, have retained master's-level first professional degrees, such as the Master of Architecture (M.Arch.) and Master of Fine Arts (M.F.A.), rather than adopting the doctorate title. However, there is ongoing debate in some fields, such as architecture, about renaming these degrees to reflect their advanced nature. In many professions, a distinction is made between first professional degrees, advanced professional degrees, and terminal academic research degrees. A first professional degree is typically required by law or custom to practice the profession without limitation. Advanced professional degrees provide specialized training in a specific area of the profession, while terminal academic research degrees focus on scholarly research and contribute to the academic body of knowledge in the field. For example, in dentistry, the first professional degree might be a Doctor of Dental Surgery (D.D.S.) or Bachelor of Dental Surgery (B.D.S.), while advanced degrees include the Master of Science in Dentistry (M.S.D.) or Doctor of Clinical Dentistry (DClinDent). In medicine, advanced degrees include the Master of Surgery (M.S., M.Ch.) or research-focused doctorates like the Ph.D. in medical sciences. Similarly, in engineering, advanced degrees include the Master of Engineering (M.Eng.) or research doctorates like the Ph.D. Below are examples of first professional degrees across various fields: Medicine: M.D., MBBS, MBChB, MDCM Law: J.D., LL.B., B.C.L. Dentistry: D.D.S., D.M.D., B.D.S. Pharmacy: Pharm.D., B.Pharm. Engineering: B.E., B.Eng., B.S.E. Architecture: B.Arch., M.Arch. Physical Therapy: D.P.T., M.S.P.T. Veterinary Medicine: D.V.M., B.V.Sc. Fine Arts: M.F.A., B.F.A. Social Work: B.S.W., M.S.W. Education: B.Ed., M.Ed. Psychology: Psy.D., Ph.D. Business Administration: M.B.A., B.B.A. Advanced professional degrees, which provide further specialization, include: Medicine: M.S., M.Ch., Ph.D. Dentistry: M.S.D., DClinDent Engineering: M.Eng., Ph.D. Education: Ed.D., D.Ed. Business Administration: D.B.A. Psychology: Psy.D. Ministry: D.Min., Th.D. In summary, first professional degrees are essential qualifications for entering regulated professions, while advanced and terminal degrees allow for further specialization or academic research within those fields.
